itinerary.cal: No permit is required, just a self-issue wilderness pass.

days.note: Walk or bike the 16 closed miles of Suiattle River Road from the washout to the Downey Creek trailhead first. From the Downey Creek trailhead (~1,450 ft), follow Downey Creek Trail then Bachelor Creek Trail (expect brush and downed trees) to Cub Lake, then continue up talus and snow to a camp on Itswoot Ridge with running water and the first full view of Dome Peak. This leg typically takes 7-9.5 hours depending on trail conditions and pace.
days.title: Approach to high camp
days.objective: Reach Itswoot Ridge / Cub Lake camp (~6,200 ft)

days.note: An alpine start to cross the basin and gain the Dome Glacier while the snow is firm, then rope up for the crevassed glacier crossing on roughly a 115° bearing to the notch at 8,560 ft, finishing with a short snow slope and a 500 ft rock arête to the summit. Trip reports agree this round trip from camp typically runs 6-8 hours.

bivy.name: Kennedy Ridge and the Glacier Creek camps, Suiattle side
bivy.notes: This is the base for Glacier Peak's Kennedy Glacier and for the Frostbite Ridge line above it, and it is also reached from the Suiattle side. The walk in from there is long even when the road is open — the Suiattle River trail runs about seven miles to the river bridge and the crest trail then carries you south toward Kennedy Ridge, so this is a full day before the climbing camp is even in sight. Kennedy Creek has no bridge and will not get one; the standard tactic is to camp short of it and cross in the morning when the flow is at its lowest, using whatever logs are in place rather than wading the main channel. Above the forest the route climbs the ridge and the glacier toward the saddle between the Kennedy and Vista glaciers at around 8,000 feet, where bivouac sites exist for parties willing to sleep on snow and rock with no shelter and no clean water. With the road washed out the trailhead is normally reachable on foot or by bike from the closure point, which adds roughly eighteen miles each way to an approach that was already the longest on the mountain, and a fire closure has also shut the upper Suiattle River Road, the Suiattle River Trail and the PCT from Mica Lake north; check with the Darrington Ranger District before planning this way in.
bivy.water: Glacier Creek and Kennedy Creek are both right there and both silty with glacial flour — let it settle or filter accordingly. Higher on the ridge water disappears entirely by late season and has to be carried or melted.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Suiattle road end. Stove only above the forest. Check the road order before driving: the Suiattle River road washed out about four and a half miles in during the December 2025 storms and is closed to vehicles at that point under a closure order that runs into 2028 unless lifted sooner, with the campgrounds and trailheads up the road closed.
bivy.capacity: Forested sites in ones and twos scattered along the crest trail near the creek crossings, plus rougher bivouac ground higher on the ridge; nothing organised, and no single site takes a large party

approach_variants.notes:
The historic line starts at the White Chuck River Trailhead at the end of FR-23 and follows Trail #643 about four miles, then Kennedy Ridge Trail #639 for 1.7 miles to the Pacific Crest Trail near 5,000 ft. Turn north on the PCT and follow it about two miles to the Glacier Creek crossing, where there are established camps with reliable water near 5,300 ft. Four to five hours is the usual pack-in.

FR-23 has been closed from milepost 3.7 to its end, so the reliably open option in recent seasons has been the North Fork Sauk Trail and the PCT over Red Pass to the same Glacier Creek camps. That is a much longer walk to the same place, and it changes nothing above camp.

approach_variants.baseFinding:
The start of the climb is below you, not above you, and that is the whole test. From the Glacier Creek camp the climbers' trail climbs a gully to the crest of Kennedy Ridge — and then you go down off the far side, to climber's right, to the foot of the Kennedy Glacier. A party that tops the ridge and keeps climbing has left the route. If you have not lost height since the ridge crest, you have not reached the base.

Arrival: the foot of the glacier, where ridge ground runs out into ice. Rope up there. On the lower glacier keep right; on the upper glacier take the centre. That right-then-centre sequence is worth memorising before you leave camp, because the upper Kennedy is a maze and there is nothing to sight on inside it.

The discriminator against Frostbite Ridge, which shares this mountain flank and this camp: Frostbite rounds Kennedy Peak to the saddle between the Vista and Kennedy glaciers at about 8,000 ft, climbs the Kennedy to a saddle at about 8,800 ft, and then leaves the ice for the ridge. This route never leaves the ice. If you are standing on a saddle looking for a rock crest to follow, you are on Frostbite. If you are still roped on glacier at 9,500 ft heading for a bergschrund, you are on this one.

The top end, and it is a real decision point: the bergschrund sits at the head of the glacier. Reach it by climbing left to the top of a snow dome and looking for a bridge from there — do not walk the schrund's length hunting for a gap at its lowest point. Above it the headwall runs about 40 degrees; stay left of, but close to, the prominent rock outcrops, and that puts you on the crater rim.

bivy.name: Kennedy Ridge and the Glacier Creek camps, Suiattle side
bivy.notes: This is the base for Glacier Peak's Kennedy Glacier and for the Frostbite Ridge line above it, and it is also reached from the Suiattle side. Kennedy Creek has no bridge and will not get one; the standard tactic is to camp short of it and cross in the morning when the flow is at its lowest, using whatever logs are in place rather than wading the main channel. Above the forest the route climbs the ridge and the glacier toward the saddle between the Kennedy and Vista glaciers at around 8,000 feet, where bivouac sites exist for parties willing to sleep on snow and rock with no shelter and no clean water. With the road closed to vehicles from milepost 12 the trailhead is reachable on foot or by bike from the gate, which adds about eleven miles each way to an approach that was already the longest on the mountain, and fire closures have affected the Suiattle River Trail and the PCT north of Mica Lake in recent seasons; check with the Darrington Ranger District before planning this way in.
bivy.water: Glacier Creek and Kennedy Creek are both right there and both silty with glacial flour — let it settle or filter accordingly. Higher on the ridge water disappears entirely by late season and has to be carried or melted.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Suiattle road end. Stove only above the forest. Check the road order before driving: the Suiattle River road is closed to vehicles from milepost 12 to its end under an order in effect since November 5, 2026, so the road end is about eleven miles past the gate.
bivy.capacity: Forested sites in ones and twos scattered along the crest trail near the creek crossings, plus rougher bivouac ground higher on the ridge; nothing organised, and no single site takes a large party

before.approach: From the Downey Creek Trailhead (1,400', end of the drivable Suiattle River Road/FR-26 — the road has been closed to vehicles at a flood washout near milepost 4, roughly 16 miles short of the trailhead; while it stays closed, add that road walk or ride to the hike and check its status first), follow Downey Creek Trail #768. The maintained tread climbs gently along Downey Creek, crossing five tributary creeks (one draining Downey/Pilot Lakes can be a difficult ford in spring high water) and passing informal camps at roughly 1.6, 3, 3.5, and 4 miles before reaching the Bachelor Creek crossing at 6.6 miles/2,400'. Expect old-growth blowdown across the tread in places and a brushy avalanche-chute crossing opposite Green Mountain. At Bachelor Creek, leave the maintained trail and pick up the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers'/boot path, which follows the north side of the creek (parties report an improved use-trail here that avoids older brushy sections) up to Bachelor Flats and Bachelor Meadows — the common first-night camp and most parties' Day 1 stop. From Bachelor Meadows continue up steepening open slopes to Cub Pass, then drop about 700' to Cub Lake and cross the meadows beyond it to gain Itswoot Ridge/Itswoot Pass. From Itswoot Pass, step onto the Dome Glacier and rope up for crevasse-hazard glacier travel, traversing to the broad Chikamin-Dome col (~8,500'), a well-established, wind-sheltered camp used as a high camp by most parties (over 7,000 ft of cumulative gain from the trailhead to this point). From the col, a further descending traverse (roughly 90 minutes) drops onto the Chikamin Glacier to a snow bench/rock outcrop around 7,000-7,500' directly below Gunsight's west face — many parties move camp here or simply day-climb from the col. Route-finding on the unmaintained Bachelor Creek path and Cub Pass/Itswoot Ridge sections, plus crevasse hazard on the Dome and Chikamin Glaciers, are the main approach-specific concerns; carry a rope, crevasse rescue gear, and be comfortable with off-trail alpine travel.

after.approach: From the Downey Creek Trailhead (1,400', on the Suiattle River Road/FR-26 — the road is closed to vehicles at milepost 12, about 8 miles short of the trailhead; while it stays closed, add that road walk or ride to the hike and check its status first), follow Downey Creek Trail #768. The maintained tread climbs gently along Downey Creek, crossing five tributary creeks (one draining Downey/Pilot Lakes can be a difficult ford in spring high water) and passing informal camps at roughly 1.6, 3, 3.5, and 4 miles before reaching the Bachelor Creek crossing at 6.6 miles/2,400'. Expect old-growth blowdown across the tread in places and a brushy avalanche-chute crossing opposite Green Mountain. At Bachelor Creek, leave the maintained trail and pick up the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers'/boot path, which follows the north side of the creek (parties report an improved use-trail here that avoids older brushy sections) up to Bachelor Flats and Bachelor Meadows — the common first-night camp and most parties' Day 1 stop. From Bachelor Meadows continue up steepening open slopes to Cub Pass, then drop about 700' to Cub Lake and cross the meadows beyond it to gain Itswoot Ridge/Itswoot Pass. From Itswoot Pass, step onto the Dome Glacier and rope up for crevasse-hazard glacier travel, traversing to the broad Chikamin-Dome col (~8,500'), a well-established, wind-sheltered camp used as a high camp by most parties (over 7,000 ft of cumulative gain from the trailhead to this point). From the col, a further descending traverse (roughly 90 minutes) drops onto the Chikamin Glacier to a snow bench/rock outcrop around 7,000-7,500' directly below Gunsight's west face — many parties move camp here or simply day-climb from the col. Route-finding on the unmaintained Bachelor Creek path and Cub Pass/Itswoot Ridge sections, plus crevasse hazard on the Dome and Chikamin Glaciers, are the main approach-specific concerns; carry a rope, crevasse rescue gear, and be comfortable with off-trail alpine travel.

before.approach: Lizard Mountain has no trailhead of its own. It is climbed from a camp at White Rock Lakes, which parties reach from the north over the first half of the Ptarmigan Traverse and leave the same way. Start at the Cascade Pass Trailhead (~3,600 ft) at the end of the Cascade River Road, 23 miles from Marblemount. The maintained trail switchbacks about 3.7 miles and 1,800 ft up to Cascade Pass (5,392 ft), the last built tread of the trip. From the pass a climbers' path traverses south-southeast across the flank of Mixup Peak to the Cache Glacier; rope up for the glacier to Cache Col (~6,900 ft), then drop to Kool-Aid Lake (~6,100 ft), the usual first camp. Beyond the lake the Red Ledge crosses the cliff band, and a roped crossing of the Middle Cascade Glacier leads to the gap beside Spider Mountain and down to Yang Yang Lakes (~5,800 ft). From there climb onto the Le Conte Glacier, work around Sentinel Peak, cross the broad South Cascade Glacier and top out at Lizard Col (~6,800 ft) on Lizard's south ridge, then descend to White Rock Lakes (~6,200 ft). From camp, regain the col and follow the south ridge roughly 600 vertical feet to the summit, a short but loose Class 2-3 scramble; stay near the crest to avoid the worst rubble on the flanks. Most parties take three days to reach White Rock Lakes, and the whole outing is about 35 miles round trip with some 11,000 ft of cumulative gain. The southern approach from the Downey Creek Trailhead is not usable at present: the Suiattle River Road has been closed at the milepost 4 washout since the 2025 floods, and washouts cut off the trailhead; check status before planning on it.
before.descent: Reverse the Class 3 scramble to Lizard Col and drop back to the White Rock Lakes camp; there is no separate descent trail, though the west ridge is a common way back down to the col. From camp, retrace the way in: over Lizard Col and across the South Cascade and Le Conte Glaciers to Yang Yang Lakes, over the Middle Cascade Glacier and along the Red Ledge to Kool-Aid Lake, then up to Cache Col and down to Cascade Pass and the trailhead. Plan on three days from camp back to the car. The old southern exit over Spire Col and down Bachelor Creek to the Downey Creek Trailhead is cut off while the Suiattle River Road is closed.

approach_variants.name: From the north — Cascade Pass and the glacier corridor
camps: Crest bivouacs above the South Cascade and Chickamin glaciers
approach_variants.notes: Lizard has no trailhead of its own and is normally met partway through the high traverse rather than approached. From the Cascade River Road end, the maintained trail switchbacks up a forested rib and then traverses meadow and talus to Cascade Pass, which is the last built tread of the trip. Leave it there and work south and east across the Mixup flank on boot path, talus and snow to the Cache Glacier and Cache Col, then drop the steep snow on the far side to the tarn at Kool-Aid Lake. Beyond, the Red Ledge cuts the cliff band west of Art's Knoll, then the Middle Cascade Glacier leads to the Spider-Formidable col and down to Yang Yang Lakes. From there the line climbs past Le Conte Mountain, crosses the Le Conte Glacier to the gap north of Sentinel Peak, and crosses the South Cascade Glacier to the col at its head before dropping into the White Rock Lakes basin. Lizard is the side trip from that camp: climb back out of the basin northeast to the broad notch on the peak's south ridge.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, once the Cache Col snow has consolidated and the Red Ledge is clear of verglas; the whole corridor has to be in condition, not just the peak.
hazards: Roped glacier travel on the Cache, Middle Cascade, Le Conte and South Cascade Glaciers, with crevasses opening through late season
Steep heather above the Cache Col descent, where a slip runs out onto rock
Red Ledge can hold an open moat, verglas or fresh snow well into summer
Whiteout navigation at the Spider-Formidable col, with no bail once past Cache Col
Loose blocks on the summit ridge
Lingering snow in gullies; remote, multi-day evacuation with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: The col is the reference, and it is the only place on this mountain where you can see both basins at once. The notch you want is the broad pass in the south ridge at a little over 6,800 ft, roughly two thousand feet of horizontal distance west of the summit. Standing in it, White Rock Lakes should be below you to the southwest and South Cascade Glacier ice below you to the northeast; the ground rising off the col toward the high point is a single broad, blocky, loose ridge of only about six hundred vertical feet, and the top of it is visible from where you stand. If you cannot see both the lakes and the glacier from the notch, or if what rises above you is far more than six hundred feet, or if you have to step back onto glacier ice to keep going up, you are at the wrong gap in the ridge. Nothing on the correct line is harder than hands-on scrambling on loose blocks — if you meet a step that makes you want a rope, you have drifted off the crest onto the flanks, where the rubble is worst. Stay near the crest and keep the party out of each other's fall line rather than strung out directly below.

bivy.name: White Rock Lakes

bivy.notes: Say it plainly: these are not sites, they are wherever a party gets to. Elephant Head is the southernmost peak, standing on the divide above the lakes at the south end of the crest with big cliffs dropping east into the head of the west fork of Agnes Creek, between the ice on either side. It gets a handful of ascents in a decade and there is no established camp for it, so parties climbing it either work out from the lake basin below or level a spot on the divide and accept a dry, exposed night. The same is true of anyone caught out on the South Cascade side by weather or by a slower day than planned. The season is short and matters more here than anywhere else: July into August has the glaciers covered and the bivouac snow usable, while September brings open crevasses, bare ice and no water at all. Anyone planning a night on this ground should carry the fuel to melt snow and treat the whole thing as an unplanned shelter that happens to be foreseeable.

bivy.capacity: Whatever the party can level. Rock rings, gravel benches and snow platforms for one party at a time, scattered along the divide. No toilet and no established sites of any kind.

approach_variants.baseFinding: The col is the reference, and it is the only place on this mountain where you can see both basins at once. Climbing out of the White Rock Lakes basin you reach a broad pass in the south ridge at a little over 6,800 ft, roughly two thousand feet of horizontal distance west of the summit. From it, White Rock Lakes lie below to the southwest and South Cascade Glacier ice lies below to the northeast; the ground rising toward the high point is one broad, blocky, loose ridge of only about six hundred vertical feet, with its top visible from where you stand. If you cannot see both the lakes and the glacier from the notch, or if what rises above you is far more than six hundred feet, or if you have to step back onto glacier ice to keep gaining height, you are at the wrong gap. Nothing on the correct line is harder than hands-on scrambling — a step that makes you want a rope means you have drifted off the crest onto the flanks, which carry the worst of the rubble. Once you're camped beyond the park boundary in the Glacier Peak Wilderness (Forest Service land), no quota permit is required, but a self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead is expected.

An easy, well-graded old-growth forest trail up the Downey Creek valley to the established Sixmile Camp, used as camp one by nearly every party heading for Spire Point or the Ptarmigan Traverse. Mellow day to bank energy for the brutal Bachelor Creek day ahead.

days.note: The crux logistics day: cross Bachelor Creek and fight through notoriously dense, wet brush on the Bachelor Creek Trail to Bachelor Meadows, cross the Cub Lake pass, then follow Itswoot Ridge (staying on talus left/west of the crest to dodge towers) to the Spire Col saddle at ~7,760 ft. Crampons typically go on around 6,800 ft where snow covers the ridge; camp at the col with big views north to Dome Glacier and Dome Peak.
days.title: Grind to Spire Col high camp

schedule.detail: Early start expected given the brush and distance ahead.

Rope up / crampons on

days.objective: Reach Spire Col via Bachelor Meadows, Cub Lake pass, and Itswoot Ridge

days.note: A short, exposed technical climb from camp followed by a long hike back out. From the col, an ascending traverse onto the southeast face leads up slabs to the ridge crest, across to the west side, and along airy Class 3 ledges above 1,000+ ft of exposure to the base of the summit block, which goes at Class 4-5 to a horn that fits one person. Two 60m rappels return the party to the col, where camp is broken down before retracing Itswoot Ridge, Cub Lake, and Bachelor Meadows back to Sixmile Camp.

itinerary.cal: Best climbed June-September once Bachelor Creek brush has leafed out and snow on Itswoot Ridge has consolidated; a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit may be required for the Spire Col camp depending on exact site.

days.note: Walk or bike the 8 closed miles of Suiattle River Road from the milepost 12 gate to the Downey Creek trailhead first. An easy, well-graded old-growth forest trail up the Downey Creek valley to the established Sixmile Camp, used as camp one by nearly every party heading for Spire Point or the Ptarmigan Traverse. Mellow day to bank energy for the brutal Bachelor Creek day ahead.
days.title: Approach to Sixmile Camp
days.objective: Reach Sixmile Camp on the Downey Creek Trail

days.note: The crux logistics day: cross Bachelor Creek and fight through notoriously dense, wet brush on the Bachelor Creek Trail to Bachelor Meadows, cross the Cub Lake pass, then follow Itswoot Ridge (staying on talus left/west of the crest to dodge towers) to the Spire Col saddle at ~7,760 ft. Crampons typically go on around 6,800 ft where snow covers the ridge; camp at the col with big views north to Dome Glacier and Dome Peak.
days.title: Grind to Spire Col high camp

schedule.label: Leave Sixmile Camp
schedule.detail: Early start expected given the brush and distance ahead.

schedule.label: Cross Bachelor Creek, ascend to Bachelor Meadows
schedule.detail: Reportedly the wettest, brushiest section of the whole approach.

schedule.label: Cross Cub Lake pass onto Itswoot Ridge
Rope up / crampons on
schedule.detail: Where the ridge route hits continuous snow.

schedule.label: Arrive Spire Col, make camp
schedule.detail: ~7,760 ft; only the tip of Spire Point is visible from camp.

days.objective: Reach Spire Col via Bachelor Meadows, Cub Lake pass, and Itswoot Ridge

days.note: A short, exposed technical climb from camp followed by a long hike back out. From the col, an ascending traverse onto the southeast face leads up slabs to the ridge crest, across to the west side, and along airy Class 3 ledges above 1,000+ ft of exposure to the base of the summit block, which goes at Class 4-5 to a horn that fits one person. Two 60m rappels return the party to the col, where camp is broken down before retracing Itswoot Ridge, Cub Lake, and Bachelor Meadows back to Sixmile Camp.
days.title: Summit Spire Point, hike back to Sixmile Camp

schedule.label: Leave Spire Col camp for the base of the climb
schedule.detail: ~0.25 mi along the ridge to the start of the route.

schedule.label: Reach the ridge crest, traverse west-side ledges
schedule.detail: Class 3 with major exposure over the west face.

schedule.label: Summit
schedule.detail: Tiny horn, room for one; parties often take turns and linger over an hour total at the top in shifts.

schedule.label: Two 60m rappels back to the col
schedule.detail: Some parties rap from a lower ledge instead of the true summit horn.

schedule.label: Break camp, begin hike out
schedule.detail: Reverse Itswoot Ridge / Cub Lake / Bachelor Meadows.

schedule.label: Arrive Sixmile Camp
schedule.detail: Long day; some strong parties push all the way to the trailhead instead (skipping this camp).

days.objective: Climb Spire Point via the southwest/southeast face, then descend to Sixmile Camp

days.note: A straightforward, mostly downhill walk back down the Downey Creek Trail and the 8 closed miles of road to the car at the milepost 12 gate, closing out the ~29-mile round trip from the trailhead.
days.title: Hike out to trailhead
days.objective: Return to Downey Creek Trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A 4-day, roughly 29-mile round-trip backpack from Downey Creek Trailhead, gaining about 6,800 ft net to the 8,264 ft summit; the Bachelor Creek/Itswoot Ridge approach day is the crux of the logistics, and the summit itself is a short but airy Class 4-5 pitch with two 60m rappels to descend. Strong parties sometimes compress the return into a single long day instead of a second night at Sixmile Camp.
